document.title: scAnyOmics: Foundation-Model Distillation for Any-to-Any Completion of Multi-omics Virtual Cells

pages.text: scAnyOmics: Foundation-Model Distillation for Any-to-Any Completion of Multi-omics Virtual Cells Zhaoqi Song 1 2 * Ye Du3 * Yusuke Iwasawa1 Yutaka Matsuo1 Qian Niu 1 # 1Department of Technology Management for Innovation, Graduate School of Engineering, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, 113-8656, Japan 2State Key Laboratory of Cellular Stress Biology, School of Life Sciences, Faculty of Medicine and Life Sciences, Xiamen University, Xiamen, 361102, China 3Department of Computing, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong S.A.R., China *These authors contributed equally. #Corresponding authors: Qian Niu. Correspondence to: Qian Niu<qian.niu@weblab.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp>. Abstract Recent advances in single-cell technologies have enabled the profiling of multiple molecular modalities, including transcriptomics, proteomics, and chromatin accessibility, providing a more comprehensive understanding of cellular states. However, integrating heterogeneous modalities and predicting missing molecular information remain challenging, particularly when paired measurements are limited. Here, we introduce scAnyOmics, a generative framework that distills knowledge from a frozen single-cell foundation model into a multimodal student model. scAnyOmics integrates scRNA-seq, protein-marker measurements, and scATAC-seq into a shared representation, enabling cross-modal prediction and reconstruction of missing modalities. We assembled 690,880 cells from six publicly available studies, covering both paired and partially paired multiomics measurements, to systematically evaluate its predictive performance. We further evaluated scAnyOmics on held-out donor data, where it outperformed baseline methods across multiple evaluation metrics. Beyond cross-modal reconstruction, we explored its applications in cell-type annotation, perturbation-response prediction, and biological age estimation. Overall, scAnyOmics provides a unified framework for integrating incomplete single-cell multi-omics data and transferring pretrained biological knowledge, supporting the development of virtual cell models across diverse cellular contexts and experimental platforms. Preprint. October 30, 2026. 1. Introduction Cells are complex biological systems whose states are shaped by interactions among multiple molecular layers. Single-cell sequencing technologies now allow researchers to examine these layers, including gene expression, protein markers, and chromatin accessibility, at unprecedented resolution. Each modality provides a different perspective on cellular identity and function. Gene expression reflects transcriptional activity, chromatin accessibility provides information about gene regulation, and protein measurements reveal important functional characteristics of cells. Integrating these measurements can therefore provide a more comprehensive understanding of cellular states. However, most single-cell datasets contain only a subset of these modalities, making it difficult to build a unified representation of cells and predict molecular information that has not been directly measured. The growing interest in virtual cell models offers a new direction for addressing this challenge. Virtual cells aim to represent biological systems computationally and predict cellular properties or responses under different conditions (Bunne et al., 2024). Recent studies, such as State and ProteinTalks, have demonstrated how computational models can predict cellular responses to perturbations and capture changes in molecular states (Adduri et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). These advances highlight the potential of computational models to support biological discovery and in silico experiments. An important step toward this goal is to develop models that can integrate different molecular measurements and reconstruct missing modalities. Such capabilities would allow researchers to study cellular states more comprehensively, even when only partial molecular information is available. Recent advances in single-cell multi-omics technologies have created opportunities to develop these models. CITE1

Figure 1. Overview of the scAnyOmics framework. scAnyOmics contains four main components: (A) single-cell multi-omics input, including scRNA-seq, surface proteins (ADT), and chromatin accessibility (ATAC);(B) knowledge distillation from three frozen foundation models (UCE, scLinguist, and Atacformer); (C) multimodal student training with masked inputs and self-distillation to learn unified cellular representations; and (D) downstream applications, including cell-type prediction, continuous perturbation-response prediction, and missing-modality inference. seq enables the simultaneous measurement of gene expression and selected surface proteins (Stoeckius et al., 2017), while TEA-seq and DOGMA-seq further combine transcriptomic, chromatin accessibility, and protein-marker measurements within individual cells (Swanson et al., 2021; Mimitou et al., 2021). However, generating fully paired multiomics datasets remains technically demanding, and many existing datasets contain only partially overlapping modalities. Differences in measurement platforms and protein panels also make it difficult to combine data across studies. Consequently, computational models must be able to learn from both paired and unpaired measurements while distinguishing genuinely missing information from observed values. Several computational methods have been developed to address multimodal integration and missing-data prediction. For example, totalVI jointly models RNA and protein measurements while accounting for technical variation (Gayoso et al., 2021). MultiVI extends this approach to paired and unpaired multimodal datasets and enables missing-modality inference (Ashuach et al., 2023). Similarly, scV AEIT incorporates missingness information to integrate gene expression, protein abundance, and chromatin accessibility across heterogeneous datasets (Du et al., 2022). These methods have established important foundations for single-cell multiomics integration. Nevertheless, a key opportunity remains to investigate whether knowledge learned from large-scale pretrained models can further improve cross-modal prediction, particularly when training data are incomplete or vary across experimental platforms. Single-cell foundation models provide a promising way to incorporate such knowledge. Models including Geneformer and scGPT have shown that representations learned from large single-cell datasets can be transferred to downstream biological tasks (Theodoris et al., 2023; Cui et al., 2024). Universal Cell Embedding (UCE) further demonstrates how gene-expression profiles from different tissues and species can be mapped into a shared representation space (Rosen et al., 2026). More recently, HoloCell has explored multimodal foundation modelling for integrating gene expression, chromatin accessibility, and protein markers, including the generation of missing modalities (Jiang et al., 2026). To2

gether, these developments suggest that pretrained representations can provide useful biological information for multimodal learning. However, effectively transferring this information into a specialized model remains an important challenge, particularly when the goal is to make accurate predictions from heterogeneous and partially observed measurements. Knowledge distillation offers a practical approach to this challenge. Originally developed to transfer information from a pretrained teacher model to a student model (Hinton et al., 2015), knowledge distillation allows the student to learn from rich representations without requiring the teacher during inference. In single-cell multi-omics analysis, this approach could enable a student model to combine information from different molecular modalities while benefiting from the biological knowledge encoded by a foundation model. By keeping the teacher frozen and training a separate multimodal student, it becomes possible to investigate whether pretrained knowledge improves the reconstruction of missing molecular measurements. This strategy also creates an opportunity to distinguish the contribution of foundation-model representations from that of the student’s own multimodal learning. Evaluating these models requires careful attention to prediction accuracy and generalization. Previous studies have shown that single-cell foundation models do not consistently outperform simpler approaches across all datasets and tasks (Kedzierska et al., 2025). Similarly, recent perturbation-prediction benchmarks have demonstrated the importance of selecting appropriate baselines and evaluation metrics (Ahlmann-Eltze et al., 2025; Miller et al., 2026). Single-cell datasets also contain biological and technical dependencies, such as multiple cells originating from the same donor, which can affect performance estimates if they are not considered during evaluation (Zimmerman et al., 2021). Therefore, reliable assessment of multimodal prediction should include comparisons with established methods, evaluation across different molecular targets, and testing on independent biological samples or datasets. Here, we introduce scAnyOmics, a multi-teacher knowledge distillation framework for integrating single-cell multiomics data and predicting missing molecular modalities. scAnyOmics leverages three frozen foundation models— UCE for gene expression, scLinguist for surface proteins, and Atacformer for chromatin accessibility—to transfer modality-specific knowledge into a unified multimodal student model. Through knowledge distillation, masked multimodal learning, and self-distillation, scAnyOmics learns shared cellular representations from incomplete molecular measurements, enabling cross-modal prediction and reconstruction. We assembled 690,880 cells from six publicly available studies, covering paired and partially paired measurements of gene expression, protein markers, and chromatin accessibility. Using these datasets, we systematically evaluate cross-modal prediction and investigate how pretrained representations and different learning strategies contribute to model performance. We further assess the quality of learned cellular representations through linear and nonlinear prediction probes and evaluate model generalization across independent samples. Overall, scAnyOmics provides a unified framework for transferring knowledge from multiple foundation models into multimodal cellular representations, supporting the reconstruction of missing molecular information and the development of computational virtual cell models. 2. Results 2.1. Cross-modal reconstruction from incomplete multi-omics profiles We evaluated the scAnyOmics ability to reconstruct unseen modalities from one or two available modalities. Using 28,239 cells with matched RNA, antibody-derived tag (ADT), and chromatin-accessibility (ATAC) measurements in held-out samples, we masked the target modality and assessed all nine input–target combinations (Figure 2). Reconstruction accuracy was summarized by the median Spearman correlation across 2,000 genes or 166 antibodies for RNA and ADT, respectively, and the median area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) across 8,000 genomic bins for ATAC. We compared the UCEdistilled student, trained on 482,102 cells from the original four-study assembly, with an otherwise comparable student without teacher distillation and with the better of ridge regression and 15-nearest-neighbour prediction for each task. The UCE-distilled model outperformed the simple baselines in all six tasks with RNA or ADT as the reconstruction target (Figure 2). Across these tasks, the improvement in median Spearman correlation was approximately 0.05–0.12. The largest difference occurred when ATAC was the sole input for ADT prediction (ρ = 0.22 versus 0.10 for the best simple baseline). ATAC-to-RNA prediction also improved (ρ = 0.25 versus 0.16). Combining two observed modalities further improved RNA and ADT reconstruction in the evaluated settings: ADT prediction increased from 0.25 with RNA alone to 0.28 with RNA and ATAC, while RNA prediction reached 0.31 with ADT and ATAC, compared with 0.29 using ADT alone. The teacher-free student scored 0.07–0.14 lower than the UCE-distilled model across all six RNA and ADT tasks and was outperformed by the simple baselines in four of them. For ATAC prediction, scAnyOmics achieved above-chance performance across different input modalities, with median AUROC values ranging from 0.53 to 0.56 (Figure 2). The 3

Combining RNA and ADT yielded an AUROC of 0.53. Although performance remained comparable to the best simple baselines, these results suggest that scAnyOmics can capture cross-modal associations between molecular measurements and chromatin accessibility, providing a basis for further improving ATAC reconstruction. 4

Figure 4. Effects of foundation-model teachers and self-distillation on cross-modal reconstruction. Rows indicate the teacher configuration and columns the observed input–target task. Entries show differences relative to a student trained without teacher distillation; positive changes (blue) indicate higher reconstruction accuracy and negative changes (orange) indicate lower accuracy. RNA and ADT panels report changes in median Spearman correlation, whereas the ATAC panel reports changes in median AUROC on a separate colour scale. Values in parentheses beneath each task label give the corresponding teacher-free score. All comparisons use the same 28,239 trimodal held-out sample cells as Figure 2. 2.2. Antibody-level variation in RNA-to-protein prediction We next examined how RNA-to-ADT prediction varied across individual protein markers. In an analysis of 10,000 trimodal test cells, scAnyOmics achieved a higher Spearman correlation than ridge regression for 125 of the 166 antibodies (75.3%; Figure 3a). The median correlation across antibodies was 0.25 for scAnyOmics and 0.19 for ridge regression. The improvement was concentrated among markers with intermediate prediction accuracy, whereas several well-predicted lineage-associated markers showed similar performance under both methods. For CD19, the correlations were 0.81 for both models; for CD3, they were 0.79 and 0.77; and for CD14, 0.79 and 0.80, respectively. Ridge regression retained an advantage for 41 antibodies, including CD24. Both methods performed poorly for CX3CR1 (ρ =−0.26 for scAnyOmics and−0.30 for ridge regression). The measured-versus-predicted profiles further characterized the resolution of RNA-based protein reconstruction (Figure 3b–e). For CD19, CD3, and CD14, predicted expression separated groups of cells with different measured marker levels, consistent with the high correlations observed for these antibodies. Within those groups, however, predictions occupied narrower ranges than the measurements. This pattern indicates that performance for these markers was driven largely by differences between cellular populations, while variation among cells with similar marker expression profiles was recovered less accurately. CX3CR1 showed weak correspondence between predicted and measured values, consistent with its negative rank correlation. These results demonstrate substantial antibody-to-antibody heterogeneity in reconstruction accuracy and distinguish recovery of broad population-level patterns from prediction of finer within-population variation. 2.3. Effects of modality-specific teacher models and self-distillation To investigate how different foundation models contribute to cross-modal reconstruction, we compared scAnyOmics trained with each teacher separately (UCE, scLinguist, and Atacformer), with all three teachers combined, and with additional self-distillation (Figure 4). We used a student model without knowledge distillation as the baseline. Figure 4 shows the improvement in prediction performance for each configuration, measured by changes in median Spearman correlation for RNA and ADT and median AUROC for ATAC. Among the three foundation models, UCE provided the most consistent improvements across prediction tasks. Using UCE alone improved all six RNA and ADT reconstruction tasks, with gains of 0.07–0.14 in Spearman correlation. The largest improvement was observed when predicting ADT from RNA and ATAC together (+0.14). UCE also improved RNA prediction from ATAC alone (+0.11) and ADT prediction from RNA alone (+0.11). These results highlight the value of pretrained transcriptomic representations for predicting molecular information across different 5

modalities. Combining all three teachers also improved RNA and ADT reconstruction across all six tasks. The gains ranged from 0.07 to 0.11 for RNA prediction and from 0.04 to 0.10 for ADT prediction. Atacformer provided an additional advantage for chromatin accessibility, improving RNA-toATAC prediction by 0.06 AUROC when used alone.Selfdistillation further improved RNA-to-ATAC prediction, increasing the gain from +0.03 with all three teachers to +0.08, corresponding to an AUROC of 0.62 compared with 0.54 for the teacher-free baseline. The self-distillation model also maintained improvements of 0.08–0.11 across all three RNA reconstruction tasks. The effects of knowledge distillation varied across modalities. While UCE consistently improved RNA and ADT predictions, scLinguist alone did not improve reconstruction performance in the evaluated tasks. Adding self-distillation also reduced performance in some ADT prediction settings. Overall, these results demonstrate that foundation-model knowledge can improve cross-modal reconstruction, with UCE contributing the most consistent benefits and selfdistillation providing further gains in chromatin accessibility prediction. 3. Methods 3.1. Study design and prediction task We designed scAnyOmics as a virtual cell framework to integrate single-cell multi-omics data, including gene expression (RNA), surface proteins (ADT), and chromatin accessibility (ATAC), as presented inFigure 1A. scAnyOmics learns a shared representation of cellular states from these modalities, enabling the prediction of missing molecular measurements when only partial information is available. For each cell, we used 2,000 genes, 166 protein markers, and 8,000 chromatin-accessibility bins. Since different datasets contain different combinations of modalities, we used measurement masks to distinguish available data from missing modality. During training, measured modalities could also be hidden from the model and used as prediction targets. For protein measurements, we further recorded which proteins were measured in each cell, ensuring that unmeasured proteins were excluded from training and evaluation. scAnyOmics uses separate encoders to process each modality and combines their information into a shared cellular representation (Figure 1C). A Transformer incorporates information from other cells within the same sample group, while knowledge distillation transfers pretrained representations from respective frozen foundation model to the student model, in which we choose UCE for RNA, scLinguist for ADT and Atacformer for ATAC(Figure 1B). Separate decoders then reconstruct the molecular measurements for each modality. Once trained, the student model can infer missing modalities without requiring the teacher-foundation model. After knowledge-distillation training, scAnyOmics also aims to resolve the downstream tasks including celltype annotation and perturbation response (Figure 1D). 3.2. Datasets We assembled 690,880 cells from six Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) series profiling human peripheral blood (Table 1): GSE158013 (59,151 cells), GSE200417 (68,138), GSE214546 (367,955), GSE236422 (181,518), GSE156478 (5,527) and GSE166188 (8,591). Four series (GSE158013, GSE214546, GSE236422 and GSE166188) profiled peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) or blood-derived T cells with trimodal assays (TEA-seq or DOGMA-seq). GSE200417 compared DOGMA-seq with CITE-seq in activated pan-T cells, and GSE156478 contributed one CITE-seq library. The cohorts differ in biological state. GSE158013 and GSE214546 profiled unstimulated PBMCs. GSE200417 profiled T cells stimulated for 12 h with CD3/CD28/CD2 activator, IL-1β and IL-23, with PGE2 and/or TGF-β. GSE236422 profiled healthy-donor T cells treated in vitro with bortezomib, lenalidomide, dexamethasone or DMSO for 4, 24 or 72 h, plus an untreated 0 h sample. The GSE156478 and GSE166188 libraries were the control (16 h IL-2) arms of a CD3/CD28 stimulation experiment. The data were organized into 47 sample-directory blocks, which correspond to source libraries or processing units, not to confirmed donors. The 47 blocks derive from 44 GEO sample (GSM) accessions; for three GSE200417 DOGMAseq libraries, cells lacking an ADT barcode match were stored as separate RNA–accessibility blocks. Donor identity was available from GEO for only two series. All five GSE158013 TEA-seq libraries and both 10x Multiome libraries came from a single donor (HMN200910). The 19 GSE214546 libraries came from 16 donors and one control individual. The donors comprised eight adults aged 55–63 years and eight 11-year-old children, all female; the control individual (IMM19, male, age not reported) contributed three libraries. Donor identity could not be resolved for the other four series. The combined matrix contained 309,724 cells with all three modalities, 353,018 RNA–ADT cells, 26,094 RNA– accessibility cells and 2,044 RNA-only cells (Table 2). The RNA-only cells were GSE158013 10x Multiome cells whose barcodes could not be matched to fragment records. RNA–ADT cells arose in two ways. Some came from CITEseq libraries (GSE200417 GSM6032900 and GSE156478). The others were trimodal-assay cells without matched fragments. These included all cells from the GSE214546 6

B069 and B076 sequencing batches (14 libraries), whose fragment-file barcodes did not match the expression-matrix barcodes, and 3–13% of cells in the remaining libraries. Thus, only the five B065-batch libraries of GSE214546 contributed accessibility data. The assembly extended an earlier 633,803-cell, four-series dataset (GSE158013 TEA-seq, GSE200417 DOGMA-seq, GSE214546 and GSE236422) with 57,077 cells from eight additional blocks. The rows of the earlier dataset were left unchanged, and all added cells were assigned to training. We used the cells retained in each source’s filtered count matrices. Filtering criteria and sample annotations therefore followed each source study and were not uniform across studies. 3.3. Data preprocessing and feature harmonization We harmonized the source-specific count matrices, barcodes, fragment files and peak files into a common feature space. Features were selected only on the trimodal training cells of the four-series assembly (historical split), so that no test cells influenced feature selection. RNA. The four original series shared a 36,601-gene reference. For each gene g we computed the variance of log-transformed, unnormalized counts across the featureselection setH: uig = log ( 1 +xR ig ) , (1) Vg = max { 1 nH ∑ i∈H u2 ig− ( 1 nH ∑ i∈H uig )2 , 0 } , (2) whereH is the set of trimodal training cells andnH =|H|. We retained the 2,000 genes with the largestVg, in their original column order; these highly variable genes (HVGs) were therefore selected by empirical log-count variance. Datasets added later were mapped to this fixed panel by gene symbol rather than column position, because GSE156478 used a different (33,538-gene) reference. When a symbol was duplicated, the first occurrence was kept; genes absent from a source were filled with zero-valued columns. GSE156478 lacked 33 of the 2,000 selected genes, and no other source lacked any. The gene panel was not recalculated for later validation splits. ADT. Antibody names were canonicalized by removing terminal TotalSeq-A clone suffixes, standardizing capitalization and punctuation, and applying receptor-name aliases (for example, HLA.DR/HLADR). Isotype-control features matching IGG.*(CTRL|CONTROL) were removed. When several source features mapped to the same canonical name, the first was retained. The analysis used a fixed union panel of 166 antibodies defined on the four original series. The 116 additional antibodies introduced by the added sources were excluded, not masked; consequently, GSE156478 and GSE166188 contributed 113 and 107 of their measured antibodies, respectively (Table 1). A cell-by-antibody mask recorded which targets were measured in each cell, and unmeasured antibodies were excluded from training losses and evaluation metrics rather than treated as zero. Chromatin accessibility (ATAC). We represented accessibility with 10-kb bins on hg38 chromosomes 1–22 and X. Each fragment was assigned to the bin containing its midpoint, and each fragment-file row was counted once, ignoring the optional duplicate-count column. For bin k we defined bik = 1[cik > 0] and pk = n−1 H ∑ i∈Hbik, and retained the 8,000 bins with the largest Bernoulli variancepk(1−pk). Accessibility values were then binarized. GSE166188 provided only a called-peak matrix and no fragment file, so peak counts were assigned to the bin containing each peak midpoint before binarization. Cells without matched fragments received an empty accessibility row with the accessibility mask set to zero; this row was excluded from all losses, teacher targets and evaluations. These features describe accessibility at 10-kb resolution, not individual regulatory elements. 3.4. Sample source and training-evaluation splits We first divided the 690,880 cells into 539,179 cells for training set and 151,701 cells for test set. In datasets with multiple blocks, we reserved at least one block and approximately 20% of cells for testing. The 57,077 cells added during dataset expansion entered the original training set. We checked sample and library identifiers against the available source metadata. We could identify one donor in GSE158013 and 17 individuals in GSE214546, but could not determine donor identities for the other four datasets. Donor HMN200910 appeared in both training and test libraries. Source library GSM6032893 also contributed cells to a test block and an additional training block. We recorded these overlaps and tested a stricter grouping approach, assigning samples with unknown donor identity to their source dataset. That approach left no trimodal test cells, so the following reconstruction analyses use the original sampleheld-out cohorts. For RNA-to-ADT prediction, we selected cells with measured RNA and ADT and an available UCE embedding. We reserved one historical training sample from each represented dataset for validation (sample indices 3, 7, 26, and 38). Using random seed 17, we selected 60,000 cells for probe training, 6,000 for validation, 8,000 from the RNA– ADT test cohort, and 8,000 from the trimodal test cohort. Sampling was without replacement within each cohort; the two test cohorts may overlap. All 166 antibodies were measured in at least 30 cells in each cohort and were eligible for evaluation. Frozen foundation-model teachers and distillation targets scAnyOmics is designed with three frozen foundationmodel teachers, one for each measured modality: UCE for RNA, scLinguist for ADT, and Atacformer for ATAC. Their representations provide modality-specific learning targets for a shared student model. Figure 1 shows this threeteacher architecture. The B, B-norm, and B-tech experiments reported here used the UCE branch; scLinguist and Atacformer were not included in these training runs. For the UCE branch, the teacher produced a 1,280-dimensional embedding for each cached cell. We used principal component analysis (PCA), fitted on historical training embeddings, to reduce it to 256 dimensions. This average summarizes the UCE representations of that sample group. The UCE cache covered 633,802 of 690,880 cells. The remaining 57,078 cells, including all 57,077 newly added cells, had no UCE distillation target in the reported runs. We kept the PCA projection and scaling fitted during the original cache preparation. Embeddings computed after data expansion were not used for B, B-norm, or B-tech. The same UCE preprocessing preceded the revised validation split. The three-teacher design assigns separate distillation targets to the RNA, ADT, and ATAC branches. The architecture specifies 256-dimensional UCE targets, 128-dimensional scLinguist targets, and 192-dimensional Atacformer targets. In the complete design, each teacher remains frozen, and the student would match the corresponding target when that modality has been measured. The present experimental results describe the UCE-only implementation; the other two teacher branches require separate training and evaluation before their effects can be reported. 3.6. Modality encoders and fusion In the B and B-tech models, each modality encoder received log-transformed measurements together with a logtransformed total count. For modality m, the input was: fm i = [ log(1+xm i ); qm i ] , q m i = log ( 1+ ∑ j xm ij ) . (7) We set negative count values to zero before transformation. ATAC inputs were binary. In the baseline ADT encoder, missing antibody entries were stored as zeros, and the antibody mask was not part of the encoder input. The mask was still used to ensure that only measured antibodies contributed to training losses and evaluation, as indicated by aij. Each modality was processed by a separate two-layer neural network. Both layers had 512 units; the network used layer normalization, GELU activation, and dropout of 0.1: hm i = GELU ( Wm 2 Drop0.1[GELU(LN(Wm 1 fm i +bm 1 ))] +bm 2 ) . The code grouped these into 32 identity, 16 age, and 48 state coordinates. These are names for blocks of coordinates; the reported training objective did not separately train them to predict identity, age, or cell state. We combined information from the visible modalities using a reliability-weighted product of Gaussian experts. This gives more weight to modalities with higher estimated precision and also includes a standard-normal prior. Context from cells in the same patient sample We processed cells in groups of up to 256 drawn from the same sample. A one-layer Transformer allowed each cell to use information from the other cells in its group. The Transformer had four attention heads of width 24, a feedforward layer of width 512, GELU activation, and dropout of 0.1. Discussion We set out to test whether knowledge from a pretrained single-cell foundation model can help a smaller model fill in missing molecular measurements. Our results say yes, but with clear limits. The main finding is that distillation from UCE made a real difference. The student trained with UCE predicted RNA and ADT better than ridge regression and nearest-neighbour averaging in all six RNA and ADT tasks. The same student trained without a teacher did worse than these simple methods in four of the six. The improvement therefore does not come from the student’s architecture alone; it depends on what the student learns from the teacher. This matters because recent benchmarks have found that complex singlecell models often fail to beat simple baselines (Kedzierska et al., 2025; Ahlmann-Eltze et al., 2025). In our setting, the simple baselines were beaten only once pretrained knowledge was added. The gains were largest when chromatin accessibility was the input. On their own, ATAC data are sparse and binary, and linear models or nearest neighbours make little use of them. Once ATAC was mapped into the representation shaped by the RNA teacher, it predicted protein and RNA levels much better. In practice, scAnyOmics may be most useful for datasets that measured chromatin accessibility but not RNA or proteins. The per-antibody analysis shows what this level of accuracy means in practice. Median correlations of 0.2 to 0.3 hide a wide range: lineage markers such as CD19, CD3 and CD14 were predicted well, while some antibodies were not predicted at all. Even for the well-predicted markers, the model mainly placed each cell in the right population and reproduced less of the variation between similar cells. Predicted protein levels are therefore suited to analyses at the level of cell populations, such as labelling cell types or checking which markers a population expresses. They should not replace measured values for individual cells. Predicting chromatin accessibility remains the weakest part. Every method we tested, including ours, reached AUROC values only slightly above chance. Single-cell accessibility at 10-kb resolution is very sparse, and much of the difference between cells may be technical noise that no input can predict. Predicting accessibility for groups of similar cells, or for regions near genes, may be a more realistic goal than predicting every bin in every cell. Not every teacher helped. UCE improved RNA and ADT completion, and Atacformer and self-distillation improved RNA-to-ATAC prediction, but scLinguist lowered performance in every task. One possible reason is that antibody panels differ widely between studies, from 45 to 154 antibodies, so the protein teacher sees a different and often small part of the panel in each cell. Adding more teachers is therefore not automatically better. Each teacher needs to be checked on its own, and the weight given to each one needs tuning. This study has several limitations. First, the test cells came from held-out samples, but donor identity was unknown for most studies and one donor appeared in both training and 13

test samples, so we cannot claim that the results carry over to new individuals. Second, each model was trained once with a single random seed, so small differences, of about 0.01 to 0.02, should not be over-interpreted. Third, we compared scAnyOmics only with simple baselines; comparisons with established methods such as totalVI, MultiVI and scV AEIT are still needed (Gayoso et al., 2021; Ashuach et al., 2023; Du et al., 2022). Fourth, all data came from human peripheral blood, much of it from stimulated or drug-treated T cells, and it is not yet known how well the approach works in other tissues. 5. Conclusion scAnyOmics combines a multimodal student model with frozen single-cell foundation models to fill in missing RNA, protein and chromatin-accessibility measurements. Distillation from the UCE RNA model improved RNA and protein completion for every combination of inputs we tested and lifted the student above simple baselines, while chromatin accessibility remained hard to predict for all methods. The completed profiles capture differences between cell populations better than differences between individual cells. With donor-level evaluation, comparisons with established methods and better use of the protein and chromatin teachers, this approach could make partially measured single-cell datasets more useful for building virtual cell models.
